category.name: Supply chain & third parties
category.description: Incidents that arrive through vendors, MSPs, open-source packages, software updates, signing certificates, and partners you trust.

playbooks.name: Trojanized software update delivered by a trusted vendor
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor discloses, or you discover, that a signed update for software you run (monitoring, management, or agent software) carried a backdoor that executed with the product's privileges.

preparation: Maintain a software inventory listing every install of each vendor product with version and host
Record the update channel for each product: auto-update, internal mirror, or manual
Keep vendor security contacts and advisory feeds subscribed for all privileged software
Restrict outbound internet from management servers to an allowlist of vendor update hosts
identification: Match installed versions against the vendor's list of trojanized build numbers on every host
Hash the product binaries on each server and compare them with the vendor-published clean hashes
Search proxy and DNS logs for the advisory's beacon domains from hosts running the product
Identify which hosts actually beaconed versus only received the malicious build
Review service-account activity used by the product for logons outside its normal targets
containment: Isolate servers running the trojanized build from the network or block their egress
Block the advisory's C2 domains and IPs at DNS, proxy, and firewall
Disable or rotate the product's service accounts and any credentials stored in its console
Pause automatic updates from the vendor until a verified clean build is published
eradication: Rebuild affected servers from known-good media rather than uninstalling the product in place
Hunt for second-stage tooling on hosts that beaconed, including new services and scheduled tasks
Reset credentials of every account that authenticated through the compromised servers
recovery: Install the vendor's verified clean release and confirm hashes before reconnecting
Monitor rebuilt hosts and the product's service accounts for renewed beaconing for 30 days
Reintroduce vendor connectivity behind tightened egress rules
lessons: Measure time from vendor advisory to complete inventory of affected installs
Add an egress allowlist detection for management servers contacting unlisted domains
Decide whether high-privilege vendor updates need a staging soak period before rollout
Review the vendor's breach report and reassess the contract's security obligations

splunk.title: Hosts resolving advisory beacon domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query IN ("<ioc_domain_1>","*.<ioc_domain_2>") by DNS.src DNS.query | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Child processes spawned by the vendor product
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="<vendor_service>.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | sort - count

splunk.title: Logons by the product service account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 Account_Name="<vendor_svc_account>" | stats count values(Logon_Type) as types by ComputerName src_ip | sort - count

playbooks.name: Malicious open-source dependency running in production
playbooks.summary: Use when a package already deployed in a production service is reported as malicious, for example a maintainer account takeover that pushed a release which steals environment variables or opens a shell.

preparation: Generate an SBOM for every production service at build time and store it with the release
Pin dependencies with lockfiles and integrity hashes in all repositories
Subscribe to the ecosystem's malware advisories through the dependency scanner
Record which services hold secrets in environment variables reachable by application code
identification: Query stored SBOMs for the malicious package name and affected versions across all services
Determine which deployments ran the bad version and the exact time window it was live
Read the malicious release's diff to learn what it collects and where it sends data
Search egress logs from affected pods or hosts for the payload's exfiltration endpoint
containment: Redeploy affected services pinned to the last known-good version of the package
Block the payload's exfiltration domain at the egress proxy and cluster network policy
Rotate every secret present in the environment of affected services during the window
Add the bad versions to the internal registry proxy's deny list
eradication: Purge the malicious tarball from internal caches and build agent package caches
Check affected hosts for files or cron entries dropped by the package's install script
Remove the package entirely if a safe maintained alternative exists
recovery: Confirm rebuilt images contain only the clean version by re-scanning their SBOMs
Watch rotated credentials for use from unexpected sources over the next weeks
Notify data owners if the payload could have read customer data
lessons: Track how long the malicious version took to reach production after publication
Introduce a minimum package age policy before new releases can be consumed
Evaluate disabling install scripts in CI builds by default

splunk.title: Egress from service hosts to exfiltration endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("<ioc_ip>") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | sort - bytes_out

splunk.title: Unexpected shells spawned by the app runtime
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","python3","java") Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","curl","wget") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process

splunk.title: Deployments of the affected service in the window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb IN ("create","patch") objectRef.resource=deployments objectRef.name="<service>" | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace requestObject.spec.template.spec.containers{}.image

playbooks.name: Typosquatted package installed by a developer or build
playbooks.summary: Use when a package whose name imitates a popular library was installed on a workstation or build agent, typically running an install-time script that harvests tokens or downloads a second stage.

preparation: Route all package installs through an internal registry proxy that logs every download
Enable EDR on developer workstations and build agents with process tree retention
Publish an approved-package list for common libraries developers rely on
identification: Pull registry proxy logs to find every client that downloaded the typosquatted name
Find which repositories reference the package in manifests or lockfiles
Review the package's install script to see what files, tokens, and hosts it touches
Inspect EDR process trees on affected machines for the install script's child processes
containment: Block the typosquatted name and its publisher in the registry proxy
Isolate workstations or agents where the install script executed
Revoke tokens stored in the developer's home directory, such as cloud, Git, and registry tokens
eradication: Replace the typosquatted dependency with the intended package and regenerate lockfiles
Delete persistence the script created, such as shell profile edits or launch agents
Reimage the workstation if a second-stage binary ran
recovery: Reissue developer credentials with hardware-backed MFA after cleanup
Verify affected repositories build cleanly with the corrected dependency
Report the package to the registry's security team for takedown
lessons: Add a CI check that flags new dependencies within a small edit distance of popular names
Measure how many installs bypassed the registry proxy
Brief developers with the actual misspelled name as a training example

splunk.title: Clients downloading the typosquatted package via proxy
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/<typosquat_name>/-/*" by Web.src Web.user Web.url | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Install script child processes on developer hosts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process IN ("*npm install*","*pip install*","*setup.py*") Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","powershell.exe","sh") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process

playbooks.name: Vendor-pushed browser extension update turns malicious
playbooks.summary: Use when a browser extension your users already have installed receives an update, often after the publisher's developer account was hijacked, that injects scripts, steals sessions, or reads page contents.

preparation: Manage browsers centrally with an extension allowlist enforced by policy
Collect installed extension IDs and versions from all managed browsers into the inventory
Know how to force-remove an extension through Chrome and Edge enterprise policy
identification: List every user and device with the extension ID installed and its current version
Obtain the malicious version's manifest and code to see which sites and permissions it uses
Search proxy logs for requests to the extension's new remote script or exfiltration host
Identify SaaS apps whose session cookies were readable under the extension's host permissions
containment: Add the extension ID to the browser blocklist policy to force uninstall everywhere
Block the extension's command and exfiltration domains at the proxy
Revoke active sessions in the SaaS apps the extension could read for affected users
eradication: Confirm the extension is gone from every device by re-querying browser inventory
Clear browser profiles' cached data for affected users where policy allows
Check affected SaaS tenants for actions taken with stolen sessions, such as new OAuth grants
recovery: Re-allow a replacement or the clean version only after the publisher confirms account recovery
Require affected users to sign in again with MFA on all SaaS apps
Communicate to users which extension was removed and why
lessons: Review whether the extension's permissions were ever needed for its business purpose
Add detection for newly observed extension update hosts in proxy traffic
Set a policy to pin extension versions for high-permission extensions

splunk.title: Browser traffic to extension exfiltration host
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.user) as users from datamodel=Web where Web.dest IN ("<ioc_domain>") by Web.src Web.user Web.http_method | sort - count

splunk.title: Session reuse from new IPs after extension update
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 eventType="user.session.*" actor.alternateId IN (<affected_users>) | stats dc(client.ipAddress) as ips values(client.ipAddress) as ip_list by actor.alternateId | where ips > 2

playbooks.name: Managed service provider or RMM platform compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when your MSP reports a breach, or their remote monitoring and management tool starts pushing scripts or installers to your endpoints that nobody in your organisation requested.

preparation: Document every RMM agent the MSP runs, its console URL, and the accounts it uses in your domain
Agree a written emergency contact and kill-switch procedure with the MSP
Forward RMM agent logs and script execution history to your own SIEM
Keep an out-of-band admin path that does not depend on the MSP's tooling
identification: Pull the RMM console's job history to list scripts pushed to your tenant and who ran them
Search endpoint telemetry for processes spawned by the RMM agent in the incident window
Identify MSP technician accounts that logged into your domain from unusual sources
Check whether ransomware or remote access tools were deployed through the RMM
containment: Stop and disable the RMM agent service on all endpoints using your own management tooling
Block the RMM platform's cloud relay addresses at the firewall
Disable all MSP technician accounts and their VPN access in your environment
Revoke the MSP's delegated admin rights in your cloud tenants
eradication: Remove tools the attacker installed through the RMM, such as additional remote access agents
Reset passwords for domain admins and any credential stored in the RMM's vault
Reimage endpoints where pushed scripts executed payloads
recovery: Restore MSP access only after receiving their forensic report and remediation evidence
Re-enroll a fresh RMM tenant with new agent keys and MFA on every technician login
Validate backups were not deleted through RMM scripts before relying on them
lessons: Assess whether the MSP should have standing admin rights or just-in-time access
Add detection for RMM agents executing script interpreters outside maintenance windows
Update the MSP contract with breach notification timelines and audit rights

splunk.title: Processes spawned by RMM agents
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("<rmm_agent>.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name _time span=1h | sort - count

splunk.title: MSP technician account logons
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user IN ("msp-*","<msp_account>") by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.action

splunk.title: Remote access tools installed after compromise
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=WinEventLog:System EventCode=7045 | search Service_File_Name IN ("*anydesk*","*screenconnect*","*atera*","*splashtop*") | table _time ComputerName Service_Name Service_File_Name

playbooks.name: Vendor VPN account used by an attacker
playbooks.summary: Use when a third-party support or contractor VPN account logs in from an unexpected location, at odd hours, or reaches systems outside the vendor's agreed scope.

preparation: Tag every vendor VPN account with its owning company, sponsor, and permitted subnets
Require MFA and time-boxed activation for all third-party VPN accounts
Place vendor VPN pools in a segmented zone with firewall rules limited to their systems
identification: Pull VPN logs for the vendor account showing source IPs, geolocation, and session durations
Call the vendor's named contact to confirm whether their staff made the sessions
Map internal hosts and ports the VPN-assigned IP reached during each session
Check whether the vendor account's MFA device was recently re-registered
containment: Disable the vendor VPN account and terminate its active sessions on the concentrator
Block the attacker's source IPs at the VPN gateway
Disable the vendor's other accounts until the vendor confirms how credentials were exposed
eradication: Review systems reached over VPN for new local accounts, services, or dropped tools
Rotate credentials for application accounts the vendor uses on the target systems
Remove firewall rules that gave the vendor pool wider access than the contract requires
recovery: Issue new vendor credentials bound to named individuals rather than a shared login
Enable access only on request with sponsor approval and automatic expiry
Monitor the reissued vendor accounts with a dedicated alert for out-of-scope destinations
lessons: Count how many vendor accounts were shared, dormant, or lacked MFA
Add an alert for vendor VPN logins from countries outside the vendor's operating region
Confirm the vendor's own incident findings were received and reviewed

splunk.title: Vendor VPN sessions by source and geo
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user="<vendor_account>" Authentication.app="vpn" by Authentication.src | iplocation Authentication.src | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Internal destinations reached from VPN-assigned IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic src_ip="<vpn_assigned_ip>" | stats count values(dest_port) as ports sum(bytes) as bytes by dest_ip app | sort - count

playbooks.name: Third-party breach exposing data you shared with them
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor notifies you, or news reports, that they suffered a breach and data your organisation sent them, such as customer records or employee details, may have been taken.

preparation: Keep a register of vendors with the data classes and record counts shared with each
Ensure contracts include breach notification timelines and cooperation duties
Know which regulators and customer contracts require notice when processor data is exposed
identification: Request the vendor's written incident summary with dates, data fields, and affected record IDs
Reconcile the vendor's affected records against your own export logs to size exposure
Determine whether any shared credentials, API keys, or SSO trust exist with the vendor
Classify exposed fields by sensitivity to drive legal and notification decisions
containment: Suspend data feeds and API integrations to the vendor until their environment is verified
Rotate API keys, SFTP credentials, and service accounts you issued to the vendor
Engage legal counsel and privacy officer to start the notification clock assessment
eradication: Confirm with the vendor that the attacker's access has been removed and how
Request deletion of data the vendor no longer needs for the contracted service
Check your own systems for use of any credentials the vendor held
recovery: Notify affected individuals and regulators where legally required with agreed messaging
Offer credit monitoring or identity services if financial identifiers were exposed
Restore data feeds with minimised fields once the vendor provides remediation evidence
lessons: Review whether the vendor received more data fields than the service required
Record how quickly the vendor notified you versus the contractual requirement
Add the vendor to a higher assessment tier in the third-party risk program

splunk.title: Data exports and transfers to the vendor
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("<vendor_ip_range>") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port _time span=1d

splunk.title: Use of vendor-issued API keys after breach date
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=access_combined ("<vendor_api_key_id>" OR user="<vendor_integration_user>") earliest=<breach_date> | stats count values(uri_path) as paths by clientip | sort - count

playbooks.name: Payroll or HR vendor breach affecting employee records
playbooks.summary: Use when your payroll, benefits, or HR platform provider is breached, putting employee identifiers, bank details, or tax data at risk and enabling direct-deposit fraud against staff.

preparation: Document which employee fields the payroll vendor stores, including bank and tax identifiers
Ensure HR admin accounts on the vendor portal use SSO with MFA
Know the payroll cut-off schedule and who can freeze bank detail changes
identification: Export the vendor portal audit log for bank account and address changes in the last 60 days
Compare direct-deposit destinations against the previous payroll run to spot new accounts
Identify employees whose profiles were viewed or exported by unfamiliar admin sessions
Confirm with the vendor whether your tenant specifically was accessed
containment: Freeze self-service bank detail changes until the next payroll run is verified
Reset passwords and sessions for all HR administrators on the vendor platform
Hold disputed payments and contact receiving banks for any diverted deposits
eradication: Revert fraudulent bank detail changes after verbal confirmation with each employee
Remove unrecognised admin users or API tokens from the vendor tenant
Disable SSO trust or SCIM tokens that the vendor's breach may have exposed
recovery: Run a reconciliation of the next payroll before release with a second approver
Notify affected employees with guidance on tax-fraud and phishing risks
Re-enable self-service changes with out-of-band confirmation for bank updates
lessons: Add a delay and notification step for any direct-deposit change
Assess whether full tax identifiers needed to be stored at the vendor
Review how employees learned of the breach versus official notice timing

splunk.title: Payroll vendor admin sign-ins via SSO
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 eventType="user.authentication.sso" target{}.displayName="<payroll_app>" | stats count values(client.ipAddress) as ips by actor.alternateId | sort - count

splunk.title: Employee phishing referencing payroll after breach
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*payroll*","*direct deposit*","*W-2*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject | sort - count

playbooks.name: Code-signing certificate compromised or used to sign malware
playbooks.summary: Use when malware signed with a certificate trusted by your environment is found, whether it is your own organisation's signing certificate or a vendor's certificate that your allowlists trust.

preparation: Keep signing keys in an HSM or cloud KMS with every signing operation logged
List application control rules that trust publishers by certificate rather than hash
Know the issuing CA's revocation process and emergency contact
identification: Collect the signed malicious file and extract its certificate thumbprint and timestamp
Search EDR and Sysmon for all files signed with that thumbprint across the fleet
Review HSM or KMS signing logs to find signing operations not tied to a release build
Determine whether the key was stolen or the signing pipeline was abused to sign the file
containment: Remove publisher trust for the certificate from application control policies
Add the certificate thumbprint to the untrusted certificate store via policy
Disable the signing service account and lock access to the HSM partition
eradication: Request revocation from the CA with a revocation date before the first malicious signature
Quarantine all files signed by the certificate after the compromise date
Remove the attacker's path to the signing system, such as a compromised build agent
recovery: Issue a new certificate with keys generated in the HSM and re-sign legitimate releases
Re-enable application control trust only for the new certificate
Inform customers who validate your signatures about the revoked certificate
lessons: Require a second approver for signing operations outside the release pipeline
Add alerting for signing requests from hosts other than designated build agents
Review whether hash-based allowlisting would have stopped the signed malware

splunk.title: Executions of binaries signed by the suspect certificate
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=7 Signature="<signer_name>" | stats count values(ImageLoaded) as files dc(Computer) as hosts by Hashes | sort - hosts

splunk.title: KMS signing operations by caller
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=kms.amazonaws.com eventName=Sign requestParameters.keyId="<signing_key_arn>" | stats count by userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress | sort - count

playbooks.name: Suspected hardware or firmware implant on delivered equipment
playbooks.summary: Use when network appliances, servers, or laptops behave as if modified before or during delivery: unexpected outbound traffic at boot, firmware hashes not matching the vendor, or tampered seals.

preparation: Record vendor-published firmware hashes for every hardware model you deploy
Keep chain-of-custody records from purchase order to installation for critical gear
Enable Secure Boot and measured boot with TPM attestation where hardware supports it
identification: Dump firmware from the suspect device and compare it with the vendor's reference image
Inspect packaging, seals, and serial numbers against the shipping manifest
Capture network traffic from the device during boot before the OS loads
Find other units from the same shipment or reseller in the inventory
containment: Disconnect the suspect device and keep it powered for evidence where safe
Quarantine other units from the same batch in an isolated network segment
Block any destinations the device contacted during boot
eradication: Reflash firmware from vendor-verified media using an out-of-band programmer if required
Replace devices where firmware cannot be verified rather than redeploying them
Revoke credentials and certificates provisioned onto the suspect devices
recovery: Reinstall replacement units with attestation verified before production use
Monitor reflashed devices for anomalous boot-time traffic
Coordinate with the vendor and, if warranted, law enforcement on the evidence
lessons: Assess whether purchases should be restricted to authorised distributors
Add firmware hash checks to the device onboarding checklist
Review whether boot-time traffic would have been visible to existing monitoring

splunk.title: Traffic from the device's management interface
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="<device_ip>" by All_Traffic.dest | sort - count

splunk.title: DNS queries by device MAC or IP at boot
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns src_ip="<device_ip>" | stats earliest(_time) as first values(query) as queries by src_ip | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: SaaS vendor outage caused by a security incident
playbooks.summary: Use when a critical SaaS provider goes down and indicates or admits a security cause such as ransomware, so you must keep operating while judging whether your tenant data or integrations are affected.

preparation: Document manual fallback procedures for business processes that depend on each critical SaaS
Keep regular exports of SaaS data you would need to operate without the vendor
List every integration, token, and SSO trust between your environment and the vendor
identification: Track the vendor's status page and advisories and record each update with timestamps
Ask the vendor directly whether your tenant's data or credentials were in scope
Inventory integrations that push data or commands from the vendor into your systems
Quantify business impact per hour of outage with process owners
containment: Disable inbound webhooks and API integrations from the vendor while its state is unknown
Rotate API tokens and integration credentials you issued to the vendor
Activate manual fallback procedures for the affected business processes
eradication: Obtain the vendor's statement on root cause and removal of attacker access
Review your logs for unusual calls from the vendor's IP ranges before and during the outage
Treat any phishing using the outage as a lure as part of this incident
recovery: Re-enable integrations one at a time after the vendor confirms restoration
Reconcile records created manually during the outage back into the SaaS
Validate data integrity in the restored tenant against your latest export
lessons: Measure how long fallback procedures took to activate versus the plan
Review whether the vendor met contractual availability and notification terms
Decide whether a secondary provider is needed for this business process

splunk.title: Inbound requests from vendor IP ranges
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.src IN ("<vendor_ip_range>") by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.status _time span=1h

splunk.title: Outage-themed phishing lures
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*<vendor_name>*outage*","*<vendor_name>*reset*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject All_Email.action

playbooks.name: Malicious or hijacked third-party GitHub Action used in workflows
playbooks.summary: Use when a third-party GitHub Action referenced by your workflows is reported compromised, for example a retagged release that dumps runner memory or secrets into build logs.

preparation: Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs rather than tags
Restrict allowed actions in organisation settings to a vetted list
Stream GitHub audit logs and workflow run logs to the SIEM
identification: Code-search the organisation for uses of the compromised action and the refs referenced
List workflow runs that executed the action during the compromise window
Inspect logs of those runs for encoded blobs or secrets the payload printed
Enumerate secrets and OIDC cloud roles available to each affected workflow
containment: Block the action in organisation allowed-actions settings
Rotate every repository and organisation secret exposed to affected runs
Delete workflow run logs that contain leaked secret material
eradication: Replace the action with a pinned clean SHA or an internal fork
Review cloud audit logs for use of OIDC roles assumed by affected workflows
Check repositories for commits or releases created by the GITHUB_TOKEN during the window
recovery: Re-run builds with clean actions and verify artifacts match expected outputs
Confirm rotated secrets are in place and old values fail authentication
Notify downstream consumers if published artifacts came from affected runs
lessons: Measure how many workflows used mutable tags for third-party actions
Add a CI policy check that rejects unpinned action references
Reduce default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to read-only organisation-wide

splunk.title: Workflow runs in the compromise window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("workflows.completed_workflow_run","workflows.created_workflow_run") earliest=<window_start> latest=<window_end> | stats count values(workflow_run_id) as runs by repo

splunk.title: Allowed-actions and secret changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("org.update_actions_settings","org.update_actions_secret","repo.update_actions_secret") | table _time actor repo action

splunk.title: Cloud role use by CI OIDC sessions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity userIdentity.identityProvider="token.actions.githubusercontent.com" | stats count by requestParameters.roleArn sourceIPAddress

playbooks.name: Backdoored core system library in Linux distributions (XZ-style)
playbooks.summary: Use when a widely used compression, crypto, or system library is found to contain a maintainer-inserted backdoor in specific release versions shipped by some distributions, affecting services such as SSH.

preparation: Collect installed package versions from all Linux hosts and container images centrally
Track which hosts consume rolling or testing distribution channels
Keep SSH exposed only through bastions with logging of every session
identification: Query the package inventory for the backdoored library versions across hosts and images
Check affected hosts for whether the vulnerable service actually loads the library at runtime
Review SSH logs on affected hosts for unusual pre-auth connections or crashes
Identify internet-exposed hosts running the affected versions first
containment: Downgrade or upgrade the library to the distribution's fixed version on affected hosts
Restrict SSH on affected hosts to bastion addresses until remediated
Freeze builds of images that pull the affected library version
eradication: Rebuild container images from base images containing the fixed library
Rebuild exposed hosts if logs show suspicious pre-auth activity
Rotate SSH host keys and user keys on hosts that may have been accessed
recovery: Verify every host reports the fixed version in the package inventory
Restore normal SSH access paths after verification
Monitor for distribution advisories about related packages from the same maintainer
lessons: Decide whether production may use rolling or pre-release distribution channels
Measure time to produce a fleet-wide answer to which hosts run version X
Add runtime library loading data to the asset inventory

splunk.title: Hosts reporting affected package versions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=package source="*package*" NAME="<library_name>" VERSION IN ("<bad_version_1>","<bad_version_2>") | stats latest(VERSION) as version by host

splunk.title: SSH pre-auth connections and sshd crashes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=linux_secure ("Connection closed by" OR "preauth" OR "segfault") process=sshd host IN (<affected_hosts>) | stats count by host src | sort - count

playbooks.name: Vendor remote support session abused to access internal systems
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor's screen-sharing or remote support session is used for actions outside the support ticket, or an attacker impersonates the vendor's support to start a session with your staff.

preparation: Define which remote support tools are approved and block all others by application control
Require a ticket number and internal sponsor before any vendor support session
Enable session recording in the approved remote support platform
identification: Retrieve the support session recording and log for the suspect session
Confirm with the vendor's support desk whether the technician and ticket are genuine
List files transferred and commands run during the session on the endpoint
Identify credentials typed or displayed on screen during the session
containment: Terminate the session and uninstall the remote support client from the endpoint
Block the remote support tool's relay domains if the session was unapproved
Reset credentials that were exposed on screen or entered during the session
eradication: Remove tools or scripts transferred during the session
Review the endpoint for persistence such as new scheduled tasks or unattended access configurations
Disable unattended access settings that let the vendor reconnect without approval
recovery: Return the endpoint to service after EDR scan and review
Reschedule legitimate vendor support through the approved process
Remind the affected staff of the call-back verification step for vendor support
lessons: Add detection for remote support tools launched without a matching ticket
Review whether the help desk knew the approved vendor support process
Require just-in-time approval prompts for every vendor session

splunk.title: Remote support tool executions
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("TeamViewer.exe","AnyDesk.exe","ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","BeyondTrust*.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Child processes of the support client
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest="<host>" Processes.parent_process_name IN ("TeamViewer.exe","AnyDesk.exe","ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe") by Processes.process_name

playbooks.name: Marketing agency account compromised and posting to your social media
playbooks.summary: Use when your brand's social media accounts publish scam, crypto, or offensive posts through an external agency's access, such as a hijacked agency staff account or social scheduling tool.

preparation: Keep an inventory of agencies and tools with publishing rights on each social account
Own the social accounts and business manager under corporate identities, not agency staff
Document escalation contacts at each social platform's business support
identification: Pull the social platform's business manager activity log for the posting identity
Check the scheduling tool's audit log for which user queued the malicious posts
Confirm with the agency which staff account was used and whether it is compromised
Capture screenshots and URLs of every malicious post before deletion
containment: Remove the agency's partner access and revoke the scheduling tool's tokens
Delete or hide the malicious posts and paid promotions
Change passwords and MFA on corporate-owned social accounts
eradication: Remove unknown admins, apps, or payment methods added to the business manager
Confirm the agency has reset the compromised staff account and its MFA
Check ad spend for campaigns created by the attacker and dispute charges
recovery: Publish a statement to followers about the unauthorised posts
Restore agency access with named individual accounts and least privilege roles
Monitor brand accounts for unexpected posts over the following weeks
lessons: Require agencies to use MFA and named accounts under contract
Add alerting on new admins or partner changes in the business manager
Review time from first malicious post to removal

splunk.title: Social scheduling tool sign-ins via SSO
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 target{}.displayName="<social_tool_app>" | stats count values(client.ipAddress) as ips values(outcome.result) as results by actor.alternateId

splunk.title: Brand account mentions in web proxy for scam links
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url IN ("*<scam_domain>*") by Web.src Web.user Web.url | sort - count

playbooks.name: CDN-hosted JavaScript library compromised on your website
playbooks.summary: Use when a third-party script your site loads from a public CDN or tag provider is altered to skim payment forms, redirect visitors, or harvest credentials typed into your pages.

preparation: Inventory every external script loaded by each public page, including tag-manager injected ones
Use Subresource Integrity hashes on static third-party scripts
Deploy a Content Security Policy with report-uri collection to the SIEM
identification: Fetch the current script from the CDN and diff it against the last known-good copy
Determine which pages load the script, especially checkout and login pages
Review CSP violation reports for new destinations receiving form data
Establish when the altered script first appeared using CDN logs or web archive captures
containment: Replace the external reference with a self-hosted known-good copy or remove it
Block the skimmer's exfiltration domain in CSP connect-src and at the WAF
Purge your own CDN and edge caches serving pages with the bad reference
eradication: Remove tag-manager rules or containers that injected the compromised script
Rotate credentials for the tag manager and CDN accounts if they were the entry point
Scan all site templates for other references to the compromised provider
recovery: Work with the payment processor to identify cards entered during the exposure window
Notify affected customers and card brands according to PCI obligations
Monitor CSP reports for new unexpected destinations after the fix
lessons: Review why SRI or CSP did not block the modified script
Measure exposure window from script change to detection
Consider self-hosting all scripts loaded on payment pages

splunk.title: CSP violation reports by blocked destination
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=csp:report | stats count dc(document_uri) as pages values(document_uri) as page_list by blocked_uri violated_directive | sort - count

splunk.title: Requests to checkout pages during exposure
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.src) as visitors from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path IN ("/checkout*","/payment*") Web.http_method=POST by _time span=1h

playbooks.name: Upstream container base image compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when a public or vendor base image your Dockerfiles build FROM is found to contain a cryptominer, backdoor, or tampered binary, so every derived image and running container may be affected.

preparation: Mirror approved base images into an internal registry and pin them by digest
Record base image digests in image metadata or SBOMs at build time
Enable runtime detection for unexpected processes in containers
identification: Identify the malicious base image digests published by the upstream maintainer
Search build metadata for every internal image built from those digests
List running pods across clusters that use the derived images
Check runtime alerts for mining or outbound connections from those pods
containment: Block the malicious digests from being pulled via admission control policy
Scale down or isolate workloads running derived images with network policy
Remove the malicious base digests from the internal mirror
eradication: Rebuild derived images from a verified clean base digest
Rotate secrets mounted into the affected pods
Delete compromised image tags from the internal registry
recovery: Redeploy workloads with rebuilt images and confirm digests in the running pods
Monitor node CPU and egress to confirm mining or beaconing has stopped
Re-scan registries to confirm no images still reference the bad base
lessons: Enforce digest pinning and signature verification for base images in CI
Measure time to answer which workloads use base image X
Restrict pulls from public registries in production clusters

splunk.title: Pods created with derived image digests
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods | spath path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.image output=image | search image IN ("*<derived_image>*") | stats count by objectRef.namespace image user.username

splunk.title: Mining-pool connections from cluster nodes
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,14444) All_Traffic.src IN ("<node_cidr>") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port

playbooks.name: Unvetted AI model or plugin granted access to company data
playbooks.summary: Use when staff connect a third-party AI assistant, model, or plugin to mailboxes, drives, or code repositories without review, and it may be sending company data to an unknown provider.

preparation: Require admin consent for third-party OAuth apps requesting mail, file, or repo scopes
Maintain a list of approved AI tools and the data classes allowed in each
Log OAuth consent grants from identity providers to the SIEM
identification: List users who granted the AI app OAuth consent and the scopes granted
Review the vendor's privacy terms on retention and model training use of submitted data
Pull API activity by the app's client ID to estimate data volume accessed
Classify the data the app could reach, such as source code or customer email
containment: Revoke the AI app's OAuth grants and refresh tokens for all users
Block the app's client ID tenant-wide in the identity provider
Block uploads to the provider's API domain at the proxy if sensitive data is involved
eradication: Request deletion of submitted data from the AI provider in writing
Remove locally installed plugins or IDE extensions tied to the provider
Rotate any secrets found in content the app accessed
recovery: Offer users an approved AI alternative that meets data handling requirements
Review the app through the vendor risk process if users still need it
Communicate the policy on connecting AI tools to company data
lessons: Add detection for new OAuth grants with broad mail or drive scopes
Measure how many users granted consent before detection
Update acceptable use policy with specific AI data handling rules

splunk.title: OAuth consent grants to the AI app
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation="Consent to application." | search "<ai_app_name>" | stats count values(ModifiedProperties{}.NewValue) as scopes by UserId

splunk.title: Uploads to AI provider API domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where Web.dest IN ("api.<ai_provider>.example") by Web.user Web.src | sort - bytes_out

playbooks.name: Logistics partner email compromise used to redirect payments or shipments
playbooks.summary: Use when a freight, shipping, or logistics partner's mailbox is compromised and messages from it ask your staff to change bank details, pay new invoices, or reroute deliveries.

preparation: Store verified phone contacts for each logistics partner outside of email
Require call-back verification for any change to partner bank details
Enable external sender tagging and lookalike domain detection on mail
identification: Collect the suspicious messages with full headers and compare with prior legitimate ones
Determine whether the mail came from the partner's real domain or a lookalike
Search mail logs for all staff who received messages from the partner since the change request
Check accounts payable for payments or detail changes made after the messages
containment: Contact the partner by verified phone to report the compromise
Quarantine further messages from the partner's address pending confirmation
Freeze pending payments to the new bank details and contact your bank for recall
eradication: Block lookalike domains used in the campaign at the mail gateway
Revert vendor master data changes in the ERP to verified values
Remove mailbox rules in your own users' inboxes if they replied and were then phished
recovery: Release partner mail after they confirm their account is secured
Reconcile shipments to confirm none were redirected to a fraudulent address
Notify finance and logistics teams of the attempt with example messages
lessons: Measure whether the call-back control was followed and where it failed
Add a mail rule flagging partner messages that mention bank detail changes
Track recovered versus lost funds for the risk register

splunk.title: Messages from the partner domain and lookalikes
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user IN ("*@<partner_domain>","*@<lookalike_domain>") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject | sort - count

splunk.title: Vendor bank detail changes in ERP
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="vendor" All_Changes.object_attrs="*bank*" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.object _time

playbooks.name: Backdoored cloud marketplace machine image deployed
playbooks.summary: Use when a VM image from a cloud marketplace or community AMI catalogue is found to contain an implanted SSH key, user account, or agent that phones home after launch.

preparation: Restrict instance launches to approved image IDs or internally built golden images
Tag instances with the source image ID and owning team
Enable VPC flow logs and CloudTrail across all accounts
identification: Find every instance launched from the suspect image ID across all accounts and regions
Inspect authorized_keys, local users, and startup scripts on one instance for implants
Review VPC flow logs for outbound connections the implant makes after boot
Check instance roles attached to affected instances and their CloudTrail activity
containment: Apply a quarantine security group to instances launched from the image
Deregister or deny the image ID via service control policy
Revoke instance role sessions by adding a deny policy for tokens issued before now
eradication: Rebuild workloads on approved golden images instead of cleaning the implant
Remove keys and users the image added from any snapshots kept for reuse
Rotate secrets the instances fetched from parameter store or secrets manager
recovery: Migrate data from quarantined instances after scanning it
Terminate the quarantined instances once evidence is captured
Report the listing to the cloud marketplace for removal
lessons: Enforce an allowed-images policy with organisation guardrails
Add detection for RunInstances using image owners outside the approved list
Review why the marketplace image was chosen over the golden image

splunk.title: Instances launched from suspect image
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=RunInstances "<suspect_ami_id>" | stats count values(responseElements.instancesSet.items{}.instanceId) as instances by recipientAccountId awsRegion userIdentity.arn

splunk.title: Outbound connections from affected instances
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudwatchlogs:vpcflow src_ip IN (<instance_ips>) action=ACCEPT | stats count sum(bytes) as bytes by src_ip dest_ip dest_port | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Instance role API activity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.arn="*assumed-role/<instance_role>/*" | stats count by eventName sourceIPAddress | sort - count
